I am fifty-two years old, and I have worked these fields in Quzhou since I was a young boy. My father taught me everything I know about farming — I never went to school, but I know the smell of rain on dry soil and I can tell when the wheat needs water just by looking at the color of the leaves. Here on the North China Plain, we get two crops from the same piece of ground if we do not waste a single day.

My wheat is already in the ground from last October. I always plant winter wheat — that is the root of everything here. I have about eight mu of land in total. Six mu I keep in the wheat–summer maize rotation, because that rotation feeds my family and gives us grain to sell. The other two mu I plant with cotton, because cotton brings cash money that pays for medicine, school fees, and repairs to the house.

For the wheat, I bought improved seed from the dealer in town — not the most expensive kind, but the kind my neighbors use and trust. Before planting last autumn I rotary-tilled the soil to break up the corn stubble and level the field. Now that spring has come and the wheat is greening up, I will topdress with nitrogen when the shoots are strong, and I will run the irrigation pump three times before harvest. The groundwater is deep here but the pump still works. I will spray four times for pests and weeds — aphids and rust always come if you are lazy. I expect about 1000 jin of wheat per mu, which is what I usually get.

As soon as the wheat is cut in early June, I will plant hybrid maize seed the very same day. There is no time to rest. I will not till the soil for the maize — I plant directly into the wheat stubble, like everyone has learned to do now, to save diesel and time. The hybrid grows fast and strong. I will irrigate twice, once at planting and once when the tassels come out, and spray three times for insects and weeds. I expect about 1100 jin per mu from the maize.

The two mu of cotton need more care than I would like at my age, but the price is good. I will rotary-till that field and plant improved cotton seed in April. Cotton drinks water and must be sprayed many times — probably fourteen times or more — because the bollworms and aphids never give up. I will irrigate twice when the weather turns dry. Picking cotton is hard on my back, but my wife helps, and we manage. I expect about 550 jin of cotton per mu.

This is the same plan I have followed for thirty years. I do what my father did, and I do what my neighbors do. We watch each other’s fields, and when everyone is planting, I plant too.
